sm: John Donvan opens the Open to Debate program at Johns Hopkins, asking whether generative AI will enhance or stunt college learning. He notes that about half of college students use AI regularly, raising worries about cheating and cognitive offloading, alongside concern that graduates without AI skills will be unprepared. Agora Institute director Ruthie Bronstein and professor Stephanie Hicks explain the partnership and the symposium that preceded the debate. Donvan then introduces the four debaters. Gary Marcus, Cathy O'Neil, Ravi Pendse, and Eddie Maloney, who joined late in place of an ill colleague, are each introduced by their background.

Donvan explains the audience will vote before and after the debate, and the side that persuades more people wins. Gary Marcus opens for stunting, arguing current systems are pattern matchers that are often wrong, and that most students use chatbots passively, a habit he calls cognitive surrender. He would introduce AI only after students have learned their profession. Ravi Pendse opens for enhancing, saying AI can offer help at scale to students, including those with disabilities, if used responsibly with humanity at the center. He says the answer to false information and bias is AI literacy, transparency and accountability, not avoidance.

Cathy O'Neil argues that learning is uncomfortable friction, and AI removes it. She says learning depends on a feedback loop of parents, teachers and peers pushing students, and good grades produced by AI break that loop. She says this will fail most for kids without tutors, small classes or intellectual support at home, because many parents treat school like a babysitting service. Eddie Maloney begins his opening by noting that universities were created to reduce friction in access to learning, bringing books, experts and laboratories together, though friction is also fundamental to learning itself.

Maloney continues that lectures, essays and exams exist because they scale, and AI can now eliminate friction completely. He compares about eighteen hundred hours of college classroom time with eight to nine thousand hours of one-to-one apprenticeship for a master electrician. He says AI is forcing higher education to rethink its structures and put learning first. Donvan summarizes both sides, then Marcus says doing it right is better but hard, and most students will use AI as a shortcut. Pendse replies that generalizing students as lazy is wrong, and faculty must design challenging experiences.

Pendse cites a Harvard randomized trial with about one hundred ninety-four physics students, in which a well-designed AI tool helped them learn faster than an active learning class. O'Neil says big tech companies are hijacking young people's brains before critical thinking develops, and AI extends what social media and phones have done. Maloney says misuse is an indictment of how we use tools, not of the tools, and says his own college-age children use AI as tutors and debate partners. Marcus says the temptation to outsource makes AI a net negative. O'Neil adds that the best answers so far, blue book tests and oral exams, have nothing to do with AI.

O'Neil says we should not solve AI problems with AI, comparing that to Mark Zuckerberg promising to fix fake news with AI. Pendse says classroom policy belongs to each faculty member, and students are adults who should be treated with trust. Marcus says he would ban it in a dictatorship, but instead suggests having students critique chatbot essays for hallucinations. He separates harmful bureaucratic friction from the necessary friction of learning that you were wrong. Maloney says inequity from access to expensive models exists, and the response should be to design for equity rather than ban tools.

Maloney says oral exams and eloquence were once central to education and are returning. O'Neil tells of a friend at UMass Boston who has students read their ChatGPT drafts aloud so they see they cannot pronounce or understand the words. Audience questions begin. Natalie, a Hopkins senior, asks why students feel driven to use AI. Maloney cites overloaded schedules with internships, double majors and jobs, while Marcus adds competition and fear of being the chump. Pendse says faculty must design experiences that reduce that pressure. A student asks how AI will change the length and physical role of college.

Maloney says time is higher education's greatest asset, and that institutions that fail to adapt may become obsolete. Marcus says four years is not magical and he would welcome three if AI helped. A Hopkins computer science professor and an alumnus ask questions, including whether college learning is the institution or the experience. O'Neil notes that online courses never replaced teachers because under ten percent finish and people learn through relationships. Maloney says human dignity, not unique ability, is why humans stay central. A K-12 teacher asks whether the horse has left the barn, and O'Neil says AI is now permanent and creates more work for educators.

O'Neil answers a high school student by suggesting that friends agree together not to use AI, saying it is unfair to put the burden on students. Pendse says to prioritize with counselors and teachers, and to treat mistakes by college adults as teachable moments. A writer asks about universities building Socratic AI tutors. Maloney says such tools exist, citing the Harvard physics course with large gains, while Marcus doubts current language models can do it. An alumna asks who ensures AI works for students without support, and O'Neil says it is the unregulated Wild West. Another student asks if AI is just another technology scare, and Pendse says the difference is speed, citing Michigan's own guardrailed tools.

Marcus says college students are smart and will find AI is not working, partly because it has invaded the job market. Closing statements begin. Marcus says students are guinea pigs in an experiment they did not sign up for, and everyone agrees on rethinking pedagogy because the current AI is harming many students. Maloney compares past fears about writing, the printing press and the internet, and says we must decide what to value going forward, since students can stunt their own learning without technology. O'Neil says the answer is political, suggesting free community college with small classes and personal attention, which she wants but doubts will happen. Pendse tells of a Michigan neurosurgeon whose AI technique left under four percent of a tumor instead of twenty-five percent.

Pendse finishes by urging everyone to be a student of AI, working with faculty, students and institutions to shape it rather than leaving that power to Silicon Valley. Donvan shares a story about a GPS failing, and the debaters discuss cognitive offloading. Maloney says writing is itself offloading, while Marcus says writing is how he learns and engages more deeply. Representatives of the Hopkins Political Union describe their group. The vote before was twenty-six point four percent enhance, thirty-eight percent stunt and thirty-five point six undecided. After, it was thirty-nine point five enhance, forty point three stunt and twenty point two undecided, so the enhance side won by moving up thirteen point one points.
